section_title: What does David accept when Ziba brings supplies?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 When David had gone a little beyond the summit, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth was there to meet him. He had a pair of saddled donkeys loaded with two hundred loaves of bread, a hundred clusters of raisins, a hundred summer fruits, and a skin of wine. 2 “Why do you have these?” asked the king. Ziba replied, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride, the bread and summer fruit are for the young men to eat, and the wine is to refresh those who become exhausted in the wilderness.” 3 “Where is your master’s grandson?” asked the king. And Ziba answered, “Indeed, he is staying in Jerusalem, for he has said, ‘Today, the house of Israel will restore to me the kingdom of my grandfather.’” 4 So the king said to Ziba, “All that belongs to Mephibosheth is now yours!” “I humbly bow before you,” said Ziba. “May I find favor in your eyes, my lord the king!”

context_lines: Just beyond the summit, Ziba meets David with donkeys and substantial supplies for the journey. He explains that they are for the royal household and those becoming exhausted in the wilderness.

When David asks about Mephibosheth, Ziba claims that he has remained in Jerusalem hoping to regain Saul’s kingdom. David immediately assigns Mephibosheth’s property to Ziba. The gift brings practical help, but the decision also accepts a serious accusation while the accused man is absent.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_samuel/16.htm) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/16.htm) understand Ziba’s report as slander. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-second-book-of-samuel/) criticizes David’s judgment as hasty because he condemns Mephibosheth without hearing him. In [2 Samuel 19:24–30](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_samuel/19.htm), Mephibosheth later gives a different account, saying that Ziba deceived and slandered him.

This scene itself reports what Ziba says, not independent proof that Mephibosheth is plotting to take the throne. Reading the accusation as an accusation preserves the question that David should have examined before awarding the estate.
